LANCELOTVS BRVNIVS MEDICVS REGINEVS IOANNI GERARDO CHIRVRGO peritissimo, & rei herbariae callentissimo S.D.P.

CVm singularum medicinae partium cognitio atque intelligentia libero homine digna censenda est; tum earum nulla vel antiquitate, vel dignitate, vel vtilitate, vel denique iucunditate, cum stirpium cognitione iure comparari debet. Antiquissimam eam esse ex eo liquet, quod quum caeterae medicinae partes (sicut reliquae etiam artes) ab ipsis hominibus (prout eos dura pressit necessitas) primum excogitatae & inuentae fuerunt: sola herbarum arborumque cognitio ante hominem formatum condita, eidemque mox creato ab ipso mundi architecto donata videri potest. Cuius tanta apud antiqua secula existimatio ac dignitas erat, vt & ipsius inuentionem sapientissimo Deorum Apollini veteres tribuerint, & reges celeberrimi in stirpium viribus indagandis studium laboremque suum consumere, summae sibi apud posteros laudi honorique futurum censuerint. Iam vero plantarum vtilitas, atque etiam necessitas, adeo late patet, vt eius immensitatem nullius vel acutissimi hominis animus capere, nedum meus calamus exprimere queat. Stirpium enim complurimae nobis in cibos, alimentumque cedunt: innumerae aduersus morbos remedia suppeditant: ex alijs domos, naues, instrumenta tam bellica quam rustica fabricamus: aliquot etiam earum vestes nostris corporibus subministrant. In quibus singulis recensendis diutius persistere, hominis esset intemperanter abutentis & otio & literis. Quantas autem, & quam varias voluptates ex stirpium siue amoenitate oculis capiamus, siue fragrantia naribus hauriamus, sine summa in earum conditorem impietate inficiari non possumus. Adeo vt absque stirpium ope & subsidio vita nobis ne vitalis quidem haberi debeat.

Quum igitur res plantaria reliquis omnibus medicinae partibus antiquitate antecedat, dignitate nulli cedat, vtilitate insuper oblectationeq; caeteras longe superet, quis futurus est, adeo, aut insensatus vt non exploratum habeat, aut ingratus vt non ingenue agnoscat, quanta vniuersis Anglis commoda, quantasque voluptates tuus mi Gerarde in stirpium inuestigatione & cultu labor indefessus, studium inexhaustum, immensique sumptus hoc de stirpibus edito libro allaturi sunt. Macte itaque ista tua virtute, istoque de republica bene merendi studio, & quod insigni tua cum laude ingressus es virtutis gloriaeque curriculum, eidem insiste animose & gnauiter, neque a re plantaria promouenda prius desiste, quam eam a te ad vmbilicum iam ferme productam ipse plene absoluas atque perficias. Sic enim & tibi adhuc superstiti gloriam paries immortalem, & post obitum tantam tui nominis celebritatem relinques, vt tuarum laudum posteros nostros nulla vnquam captura sit obliuio. Bene vale.

Ex Aula Reginea Westmonasterij, ipsis Calendis Decemb. 1597.
results.translation:
LANCELOT BROWNE, PHYSICIAN TO THE QUEEN, TO JOHN GERARD, SURGEON, most skilful, and most learned in the matter of herbary, sends greeting.

Since the knowledge and understanding of the several parts of medicine ought to be reckoned worthy of a free man, then none of them ought rightly to be compared with the knowledge of plants, whether in antiquity, dignity, utility, or finally in pleasantness. That it is most ancient appears from this: that whereas the other parts of medicine (as also the other arts) were first devised and invented by men themselves, as hard necessity pressed them, the knowledge of herbs and trees alone seems to have been established before man was formed, and to have been given to him as soon as he was created by the very Architect of the world. So great was its estimation and dignity in ancient ages, that men of old attributed its invention to Apollo, the wisest of the gods, and the most renowned kings spent their study and labour in searching out the virtues of plants, reckoning this would bring them the highest praise and honour among posterity.

Now indeed the usefulness of plants, and likewise their necessity, is so widely spread, that no man's mind, however keen, can grasp its vastness, much less can my pen express it. For very many plants serve us for food and nourishment; countless others furnish remedies against diseases; from others we build houses, ships, and instruments both of war and of husbandry; some also provide clothing for our bodies. To dwell longer upon the enumeration of these several things would be the part of a man intemperately abusing both leisure and letters. But how great, and how various, are the pleasures we draw from plants — whether their beauty which we take in with our eyes, or their fragrance which we breathe in with our nostrils — we cannot deny without great impiety toward their Creator; so much so that without the help and support of plants, our life could scarcely be called truly living.

Since therefore the matter of plants surpasses all other parts of medicine in antiquity, yields to none in dignity, and moreover far exceeds the rest in usefulness and delight, who henceforth shall be so senseless as not to have inquired into it, or so ungrateful as not frankly to acknowledge how great benefits, and how many pleasures, thy unwearied labour, my Gerard, thy unexhausted study, and thy vast expenses in the investigation and cultivation of plants, shall bring to all the English by this book now published concerning plants. Go forward then in this thy virtue, and in this thy zeal to deserve well of the commonwealth; and since thou hast entered upon so glorious a course of virtue and renown, persist in it with spirit and diligence, nor cease from promoting the cause of plants until thou hast thyself fully completed and perfected that work which thou hast now almost brought to its very navel [midpoint]. For thus, while yet living, thou shalt build for thyself an immortal glory, and after death leave behind so great a fame of thy name, that no forgetfulness shall ever be able to seize upon thy praises among our posterity. Farewell.

From the Queen's Court at Westminster, on the very Kalends of December, 1597.

results.translation:
Thomas Newton of Cheshire, to Master John Gerard, no ordinary friend. Greeting.

After so many volumes written by learned scholars who teach to unlock the virtues of herbs, you at last come forth and diligently adorn this our Sparta, while you strive to have snatched the palm of praise from all the rest.
Nor do you do this so that you may be enriched with shining gold, nor that a great heap of wealth may grow for you;
But, wishing to do good, you range over hills clothed in grass, and over fields, and the leafy grove.
And thence, like a bee, you gather Paeonian (healing) herbs, and heap up plants into your own hive.
A thousand kinds of plants are known to you, and a thousand marks of them; your little garden at home, which you tend yourself, is proof of it.
The leafy vines, the fragrant cedar, the unwedded laurel are known to you; known too is the rich olive.
Balsams, narcissus, rhododaphne, spikenard, amomum, sage, dittany, and galbanum are known to you.
What need of more words? Root, stem, flower, branch with its bark, and the ear of corn with its husks — all are well known to you.
Therefore I congratulate you, Gerard, and with you all Britons; I congratulate also Nantwich, and myself.
For Cheshire bore both you and me as our common mother, yet you were born under a better star.
Be blessed in spirit, and press on, I pray, and drive the work you have begun still further onward. Life is lived by the mind's power.
Let others have gold, gems, and glittering rubies — write you of plants and flowers, Gerard. Farewell.

Truly and from the heart, yours, Thomas Newton of Ilford, [a Greek epithet, likely meaning 'friend' or 'lover of learning', uncertain].

---

Thomas Thorney, Master in Surgery, to his learned friend and loving brother in Art, Master John Gerard.

Oft have I heard, and oft have read, in books of learned lore, that Man bore the name of 'Little World,' or Microcosm.
And rightly so; for his mind ranges about the circled world, and his head (a little Globe) conceives every worldly thing throughout.
As this is true in all things, so now it appears true especially in thee, sweet Gerard, by this special token here in this thy new Herball.

GAze they that lift vpon the loftie skies,
As rapt with Iunoes painted peacocks traine
When in the aire fhe vaunts hir Argus eies,
And dips hir bowe in partie-colourde raine,
How firft fhe fpredes,then wraps it vp againe :
   Heauens azure curtaine let whofe will behold,
   Bedafht with aglets and with fpangs of gold.

My friend likes not to mount aboue his reach,
Or meddle there where diftance maketh dout :
High things are hard to learne and bad to teach,
And no leffe dangerous to go about :
The funne we fee puts oft the eiefight out,
   And vpright gazers minding not their feete,
   Stumbling do lay their length vpon the ftreete.

A lowly courfe more fitter for his looke
Doth pleafe him better,than thefe loftie fhowes :
The fruitfull earth he makes his daily booke,
And turnes fuch leaues as all his fenfes knowes :
He marks the fertill ground whereon he goes,
   And viewes the plentie of our mother Earth,
   Which yeelds fupplie againft difeafe and dearth.

Our mother Earth poffeft with womans pride,
Perceiuing Gerard to be beauties iudge,
And that hir treafure is not vnefpide,
Of hir faire flowring brats fhe is no fnudge :
But here and there where Gerard loues to trudge,
   Hir verdant mantle fpreading round about,
   She boafts the pleafance of hir goodly rout.

They all take Gerard for chiefe friend of theirs,
To whom they frame a garland for a figne
Of that pure loue,which each to other beares;
O let the red Rofe and the Eglantine
Vouchfafe their prefence in his garland twine:
   Let thofe faire flowers of our English field,
   Vnwitherde long their fragrant odours yeeld.

Thus far Mathiolus his owne writing of the liberalitie of Princes towards him. What age do we liue in here,that will fuffer all vertue to go vnrewarded ? Mafter Gerard hath taken more paines than euer Mathiolus did in his Commentaries,and hath corrected a number of faults that he paffed ouer,and I dare affirme in reuerence be it fpoken of that excellent man,that Mafter Gerard doth knowe a great number of fimples that were not knowen in his time : and yet I doubt whether he fhall tafte of the liberalitie of either Prince,Duke,Earle,Bifhop,or publike eftate. THE FIRST BOOK OF THE HISTORY OF PLANTS, containing Grasses, Rushes, Corn, Flags, Bulbous, or Onion-rooted Plants.

The Preface.

In this history of plants it would be tedious to use, by way of introduction, any curious discourse upon the general division of plants, contained in Latin under Tree, Shrub, Undershrub, Herb: or to speak of the differing names of their several parts, more expressible in Latin than our common tongue can well express. Or to attempt to teach thee, or rather to deceive thee, by smell or taste, to guess at the temperature (nature) of plants: whereas each of these, in its own place, shall have its true description and note, whereby thou mayest both know and use them.

In three books, therefore, as in three gardens, all our plants are arranged: sorted as nearly as might be by kindred and neighborhood.

The first book contains Grasses, Rushes, Corn, Flags, Bulbous, or Onion-rooted plants.
The second contains all sorts of herbs used for food, medicine, or sweet smell.
The third contains trees, shrubs, bushes, fruit-bearing plants, Resins, Gums, Roses, Heath, Mosses, Mushrooms, Coral, and their several kinds.

Each book has chapters, one for each herb, as a bed for it: and every plant presents thee with its Latin and English name in the title.

Then follow the kinds, description, habitat, season, names, nature, and virtues, in agreement with the best-accepted opinions.

Last of all thou hast a general Index in both Latin and English, together with a careful supplement of a bilingual index of barbarous (foreign) names.

And so, having given thee a general view of this garden, we will now, with our friendly labors, accompany thee and lead thee through a grassy plot, little or nothing touched upon by many herbalists heretofore: and begin with the most common, or best-known Grass, which is called in Latin Gramen pratense (Meadow Grass). Then little by little we will lead thee through most pleasant gardens and other delightful places, wherever any herb or plant may be found fit for food or medicine.

Of Meadow Grass. Chapter 1.

The Kinds.
There are many and countless kinds of grasses not mentioned by the ancients, either because they thought it unnecessary to record them, or because they did not know of them: they mention only a few, whose omissions we intend to supply, with such kinds as have come to our knowledge, leaving the rest to the curious searcher of simples (herbs).

The Description.
1. Common Meadow Grass has very small tufts of roots, with thick hairy threads hanging from the topmost turf, matting and creeping along the ground with a very thick and visible show of wheat-like leaves, sending up long, thin, jointed, and light stalks a foot or a cubit high, growing small and sharp at the top, with an ear that is loose and hangs downward, like the tuft or top of the common Reed called Vallatoria.
2. Small Meadow Grass differs from the former in the variety of soil it grows in: for as the first kind grows in meadows, so this Small grass clothes hilly and drier, untilled, and barren ground...

Corn grass.

Pannick grass.

The place and time.
These kinds of grasses grow in fertile fields and pastures, at the same time of year that others do.

Gramen panniculatum is called Heragrostis in Greek, and by Lobelius in Latin Gramen Tomentosum and Acerosum. Gramen sylvaticum — or, as others prefer, Gramen nemorosum — is called in our tongue Wood grass, or Shadow grass.

No medicinal virtue is ascribed to these grasses; rather, they are reckoned unprofitable, both for man and beast.

Of great Foxtail grass. Chapter 7.

The description.
1. The great Foxtail grass has many thready roots like the common meadow grass. The Description.
5. This kind of Flower-de-luce first came to us from Portugal. It brings forth in springtime flowers of a purple or violet color, smelling like a violet, with a white hairy stripe down the middle. The root is thick and short, stubborn or hard to break. In leaves and appearance it is like the lesser Flower-de-luce of Dalmatia, but the leaves spread more broadly, and it commonly has but one flower upon one stalk, which flowers again in autumn, bringing forth the same kind of flowers, for which reason it was called Iris biflora (twice-flowering Iris).
6. Iris violacea is like the former, but much smaller, and the flower is of a deeper violet color.

The Description.
7. Carolus Clusius, that excellent and learned father of herbalists, has set forth in his Pannonic Epitome a picture of this beautiful Flower-de-luce, with great broad leaves, thick and fat, of a purple color near the ground, resembling the great Dalmatian Flower-de-luce very well. The root is very sweet when dried, and rivals the Florentine Iris in sweetness. The flower is, of all the others, most confusedly mixed with various colors, so much so that my pen cannot set down every line or streak as it deserves. The three upright leaves clasp or embrace one another and are of a yellow color. The leaves that hang downward at the edges are of a pale color, the middle part white, mixed with a line of purple, with many small purple lines striped over the said white flower, even to the edge of the pale-colored border. It smells like hawthorn flowers when lightly smelled.
8. The German Flower-de-luce, which Camerarius has described in his book called Hortus Medicus, has great thick and knobby roots; the stalk is thick and full of juice; the leaves are very broad compared to all the other Flowers-de-luce. The flower grows at the top of the stalk, consisting of six great leaves, blue in color, ridged down the middle, with white tending to yellow; at the bottom next to the stalk it is white in color, with some yellowness fringed about the said white, as also about the edges, which greatly enhances its beauty. This plant Joachim Camerarius, son of the elder Camerarius of Nuremberg, sent out of Hungary, and gave one of the plants to Clusius, whose depiction and description he has most vividly set forth—differing somewhat from the one Joachim himself gave to me when he was in London. The leaves, he says, are very large, twice as broad as any of the others. The stalk is single and smooth; the flower at the top is of a most bright shining blue color, the middle rib tending to whiteness, the three upper leaves somewhat yellowish. The root is likewise as sweet as Ireos (orris root).

The Place.
These kinds of Flower-de-luce grow wild in Dalmatia, Gorizia, and Piedmont; nevertheless our London gardens are very well stocked with every one of them.

The Time.
Their flowering time corresponds to that of the other Flowers-de-luce.

The Names.
The Dalmatian Flower-de-luce is called in Greek by Athenaeus and Theophrastus 'iris' (rainbow); it is also called 'ourania,' of the heavenly bow, or rainbow; for the same reason it is called 'thaumastos,' or admirable, for poets sometimes call the rainbow 'thaumantian.' In Latin it is called Iris, and in English, Flower-de-luce. Their various titles sufficiently distinguish them, so that they may be known one from another.

The Nature.
The nature of these Flowers-de-luce corresponds to those of the common kind, that is to say, the dried roots are hot and dry in the latter part of the second degree.

The Virtues.
A. The juice of these Flowers-de-luce not only mightily and vehemently draws forth choler, but especially watery humors, and is a singularly good purgative for those who have dropsy, if drunk in sweet wort or whey.
B. The same is good for those with poor spleens, or those troubled with cramps or convulsions, and for those bitten by serpents. It also greatly benefits those who have gonorrhea or a running of the reins (kidneys), being drunk with vinegar, as Dioscorides says; and drunk with wine it brings down the monthly courses (menstruation).

THE FIRST BOOKE OF THE

Of Corne. Chap.40.

❆ The kindes.

Hus far haue I discoursed vpon Grasses, Rushes, Spartum, Flags, and Flower de-luces; my next labour is to set downe for your better instruction, the historie of Corne, and the kindes thereof, vnder the name of Graine, which the Latins call Cerealia semina, or bread corne: the Grecians σῖτος and δημήτεια σπερματα, of which we purpose to discourse. There belong to the historie of graine all such things as be made of corne, as Far, Chondrus, Alica, Tragus, Amylum, Ptisana, Polenta, Maza, Byne or Mault, Zythum, and whatsoeuer are of that sort. There be also ioined vnto them many seedes, which Theophrastus in his eight booke placeth among the graines, as Millet, Sorgum, Panicke, Indian wheate, and such like. Galen in his first booke of the faculties of nourishments, reckoneth vp the diseases of graine, as well those that come of the graine it selfe degenerating, or that are changed into some other kinde, and made worse through the fault of the weather, or of the soile; as also such as be cumbersome, by growing among them, do likewise fitly succeede the graines. And beginning with corne, we will first speake of wheate, and describe it in the first place, bicause it is preferred before all other corne.

1 Triticum spica mutica.
White Wheate.

❆ The description.

1 This kind of Wheat which L'Obelius calleth Spica Mutica, is the most principal of all other, whose eares are altogither bare or naked, without awnes or chaffie beardes. The stalk riseth from a threddie roote, compact of many strings, iointed or kneed, at sundry distances; from whence shoot foorth grassie blades or leaues, like vnto Rie, but broader: the plant is so well knowne to many, and so profitable to all, that the meanest and most ignorant, need no larger description to know the same by.

❆ The description.

2 The second kinde of Wheate in roote, stalks, ioints and blades, is like the precedent, differing onely in eare, and number of graines, whereof this kinde doth abound, hauing an eare consisting of many ranks, which seemeth to make the eare double or square eared. But it is not greatly to our purpose particularly to seek out their places of growing wild, seeing that we have them all, and every one of them, in our London gardens in great abundance. The common white Daffodil grows wild in fields and sides of woods in the western parts of England.

The Time.
They flower for the most part in the spring, that is, from the beginning of February until the end of April.
The Persian and winter Daffodils flower in September and October.

The Names.
Although their names are set forth in their several titles, which may serve for their appellations and distinctions, nevertheless it shall not be out of place to add a supply of names, as well as the reason why they are so called.
The Persian Daffodil is called in the Slavonian or Turkish tongue Zaremcada Persiana, and Zaremcatta, as for the most part all other sorts of Daffodils are. Nevertheless the double-flowered Daffodil they name Giul catamer lale, which name they generally give to all double flowers.
The common white Daffodil with the yellow circle they call Serin Cade, that is to say, 'the king's chalice,' and Deue bohini, which means 'camel's neck,' as we say of a thing with a long, spindly shank, a long shank, comparing it to the long neck of the flower.
The rush Daffodil is called by some Jonquillius, from the resemblance its leaves have to rushes; and by Dioscorides, Bulbus vomitorius, or 'vomiting bulb.'
Generally all the kinds are comprehended under the name Narcissus, called by the Greeks narkissos; in Dutch Narcissen; in Spanish Jennetten; in English Daffodilly, Daffodowndilly, and Primrose peerless.
Plutarch, in his book of Feasts, shows that they are called Narcissus as though they numb the sinews and cause drowsiness or heaviness, and therefore Sophocles names them the garland of the great infernal goddesses, because those who have departed and been dulled by death should worthily be crowned with a dulling flower.
Of the first and second Daffodil, Ovid makes mention in the third book of his Metamorphoses, where he describes the transformation of the fair boy Narcissus into a flower of his own name, saying:
  'Nowhere was there a body, but in place of a body they found a saffron-colored flower, its center encircled with white petals.'
But as for the body, none remained; instead they found a yellow flower, with milk-white leaves, newly sprung upon the ground.
Pliny and Plutarch affirm, as has been partly touched upon before, that their narcotic quality was the very cause of the name Narcissus, that is, a quality causing sleepiness, which in Greek is called narkosis: or from the fish Torpedo, called in Greek narke, which numbs the hands of those who touch it, being hurtful to the sinews and bringing dullness to the head — a property belonging to the Narcissi, whose smell causes drowsiness.

The Nature.
The roots of Narcissus are hot and dry in the second degree.

The Virtues.
A. Galen says that the roots of Narcissus have such wonderful drying qualities that they close and glue together very great wounds, and even such rifts, gashes, or cuts as happen about the veins, sinews, and tendons. They also have a certain wiping, cleansing, and drawing faculty.
B. The roots of Narcissus, stamped with honey and applied as a plaster, help those who are burnt with fire, and join together sinews that are cut asunder.
C. Used in the manner aforesaid, it helps the great wrenches of the ankles, and the aches and pains of the joints.
D. The same, taken with honey and the seed of nettles, purges the disease which causes spottiness in the body, called Ephelis and Alphus, and sunburn.
E. The same, stamped with hog's grease and leaven of rye bread, hastens hard imposthumes (abscesses) to maturity, which are not easily brought to ripeness.
F. Being stamped with the meal of cockle and honey, it draws forth thorns and splinters out of any part of the body.

THE FIRST BOOK OF THE

Of Leeks, Chapter 86.

Porrum.
Leeks.

The Description.

The leaves or blades of the Leek are long, somewhat broad, and very numerous, having a keel or ridge on the underside, and in smell and taste resembling the Onion. The stalks, if the blades are not often cut, grow up round in the second or third year, bearing at the top flowers gathered into a round head or ball, as does the Onion; the seeds are similar. The bulb or root is long and slender, especially in the unset (transplanted) Leek; the root of the other kind of Leek is thicker and larger.

The Place.

It requires a moderate soil, rich, well manured and dug over. It is very common everywhere in other countries as well as in England.

The Time.

It may be sown in March or April, and should be transplanted in September or October.

The Names.

The Greeks call it 'prason'; the Latins, Porrum. The Emperor Nero took great pleasure in this root, and was therefore mockingly called 'Porrophagus' (leek-eater). But Palladius, using the masculine form, calls it 'Porrus'; the Germans call it 'Lauch'; the people of Brabant call it 'Porrette'; the Spaniards call it 'Puerro'; the French call it 'Porreau'; and the English call it Leek or Leeks.

The Temperature.

The Leek is hot and dry in nature, and thins or attenuates the humors, as does the Onion.

The Virtues.

A. Being boiled, it is less harmful, because it loses much of its sharpness; yet even so prepared, it yields no good nourishment to the body. But when eaten with cooling herbs, its harshness is tempered.

B. Being boiled and eaten with barley water (ptisan) or barley cream, it helps to digest and bring up raw humors lodged in the chest. Some say it is good taken as a licking medicine (electuary) to cleanse the passages of the lungs.

C. The juice drunk with honey is good against the bites of venomous creatures, and likewise the bruised leaves applied to the wound.

D. The same juice mixed with vinegar, frankincense, and milk, or oil of roses, dropped into the ears, eases pain and relieves ringing or noise in them.

E. Two drams, or a quarter of an ounce, of the seed, taken with an equal weight of Myrtle berries, stops long-continued spitting of blood. Put into wine, it keeps it from turning sour, and if the wine is already sour, it corrects this fault, as many writers affirm. It also cuts through thick and tough humors.

The Harms.

178  THE SECOND BOOK OF THE

The Description.

1  The Turnip has long, rough, and green leaves, cut or notched about the edges with deep gashes. The stalk divides itself into several branches or arms, bearing at the top small flowers of a yellow color, and sometimes of a light purple; after which there follow long seed-pods full of small blackish seed like rape seed. The root is round like a ball, and sometimes stretched out a little in length, growing very shallow in the ground, and often showing itself above the surface of the earth.

2  The small Turnip is like the former, except that it is smaller. The root is much sweeter in taste, as I myself have often proved.

3  There is said to be a third sort of small Turnip having red roots, but I myself have not yet seen any such. But I am of the opinion that some have seen the root of the red Beet, which oftentimes is found in barren ground to have a root inclining toward roundness, and of a red or reddish color, which has been mistaken for a kind of Turnip.

The Place.

The Turnip thrives well in light, loose, and rich earth—so loose, as Petrus Crescentius shows, that it may be turned almost into dust. It grows in fields and various vineyards, or hop gardens, in most parts of England.

The small Turnip grows near a village near London (called Hackney) in sandy ground, and is brought to the Cross in Cheapside by the women of that village to be sold, and they are the best that I have ever tasted.

The Time.

Turnips are sown in the spring, as also at the end of August. They flower and seed the second year after they are sown; for those which flower in the same year that they are sown are a degenerate kind, called in Cheshire near Nantwich "Mad Neeps," because of their evil quality in causing frenzy and giddiness of the brain for a time.

The Names.

The Turnip is called in Latin Rapum; in Greek gongyle, which is commonly used in shops, and everywhere called Rapa. The Lacedemonians call it [gasre]; the Boeotians [zekeltis], as Athenaeus reports; in High Dutch it is named Ruben; in Low Dutch Rapen; in French Naveau rond; in Spanish Nabo; in English Turnip and Rape.

The Temperature and Virtues.

A  The bulbous or knobbed root, which is properly called Rapum or Turnip, and has given its name to the plant, is many times eaten raw, especially by the poor people in Wales, but most commonly it is boiled. The raw root is windy and engenders coarse and cold blood; the boiled root cools less, and so little that it can scarcely be perceived to cool at all, yet it is moist and windy.

B  It matters a good deal in what manner it is prepared; for being boiled in water or in a certain broth, it is more moist and passes through the body sooner, and makes the body more loose; but being roasted or baked, it dries and engenders less wind, though it is not altogether without wind. But however they are prepared, they yield more nourishment than those eaten raw: they increase milk in women's breasts, and natural seed, and provoke urine.

C  A decoction of Turnips is good against coughing and hoarseness of the voice, being drunk in the evening with a little sugar or some clarified honey.

D  Dioscorides writes that the Turnip itself, being pounded, is applied with good success upon mouldy or chilblained heels, and also that oil of roses boiled in a hollowed-out Turnip under hot embers cures the same.

E  The young and tender shoots or sprouts of Turnips, at their first coming forth of the ground, boiled and eaten as a salad, provoke urine.

F  The seed is mixed with antidotes and treacles: and being drunk, it is a remedy against poison.

G  Those of the Low Countries give the oil pressed out of the seed against the after-pains of women newly delivered, and also administer it to young children against worms, which it both kills and drives forth.

H  The oil, washed with water, soothes the fervent heat and roughness of the skin.

258
THE SECOND BOOK OF THE

Of Stinking Orach. Chapter 42.

Atriplex olida.
Stinking Orach.

The description.
Stinking Orach grows flat upon the ground, and is a base and low plant with many weak and feeble branches; whereupon grow small leaves of a grayish colour, sprinkled over with a certain kind of dirty mealiness, shaped like the leaves of Basil: among which leaves here and there are confusedly dispersed the seeds, as if they were nothing but dust or ashes. The whole plant is of a most loathsome savour or smell, upon which plant, if any should chance to rest and sleep, he might very well report to his friends that he had reposed himself among the chief of Scoggin's heirs.

The place.
It grows upon dung hills and in the most filthy places that may be found, as also about the common pissing places of great princes and noblemen's houses. Sometimes it is found in places near brick kilns and old walls, which somewhat alters its smell, which is then like toasted cheese; but that which grows in its natural place smells like stinking salt fish, whereof it took its name Garosmus.

The time.
It is an herb for a year, which springs up, and when the seed is ripe it perishes, and recovers itself again from its own seed, so that if it has gotten into a ground, it cannot be destroyed.

The names.
Stinking Orach is called by Cordus Garosmus, because it smells like stinking fish, which is called in Greek 'tarson': it is likewise called Tragium Germanicum, and Atriplex foetida garum olens by Pena and L'Obel, for it smells more stinking than the rank male goat, whereupon some by a figure of speech have called it Vulvaria, and it may be called in English stinking Motherwort.

The nature and virtues.
There has been little or nothing set down by the ancients concerning either its nature or virtues; nonetheless it has been thought profitable, by reason of its stinking smell, for such as are troubled with the Mother (womb ailment/hysteria): for as Hippocrates says, when the womb suffocates or strangles, such things are to be applied to the nose as have a rank and stinking smell.

Of Goose-foot. Chapter 43.

The description.
Goose-foot is a common herb and thought to be a kind of Orach: it rises up with a stalk a cubit high or higher, somewhat furrowed and branched: the leaves are broad, smooth, sharp-pointed, shining, having certain deep cuts about the edges, and resembling the foot of a goose. The flowers are small, somewhat red, the seed stands in clusters upon the top of the branches, being very like the seed of wild Orach, and the root is divided into sundry strings.

They flourish especially in the summer solstice, or about the time when the sun enters into Cancer.

The names.
The Grecians call it Heliotropium: the Latins keep these names Heliotropium magnum, and Scorpiurum: Ruellius calls it Herba Cancri: it is named Heliotropium, not because it is turned about at the daily motion of the sun, but because it flowers at the summer solstice, at which time the sun, being farthest gone from the equinoctial circle, returns to the same; and Scorpiurum from the twiggy tops that bow backward like a scorpion's tail: the Italians call it Tornefol bobo: in French Tournsol: it is also called Herba Clitiae, of which the poet has these verses:

Scorpion grass has many smooth, plain, even leaves, of a dark green colour; stalks small, feeble, and weak, trailing upon the ground and occupying a great space in respect of the size of the plant. The time.
This herb must be sown in April in a bed of hot horse dung, as musk melons are, and flowers in August.

The names.
Petrus Bellonius has judged it to be the Malinathalla of Theophrastus. In the Duchy of Milan it is called by the Insubres 'Melongena': and by some 'Melanzana': in Latin 'Mala insana': in English Mad Apples: in the German tongue 'Dollopffel': in Spanish 'Verangenes'.

The nature.
This herb is cold almost in the fourth degree.

The use and danger.
The people of Toledo eat them with great devotion, being boiled with fat flesh, adding thereto some scraped cheese, which they keep in vinegar, honey, or salt pickle, all winter to procure lust.
Petrus Bellonius and Hermolaus Barbarus report that in Egypt and Barbary, they are accustomed to eat the fruit of Mala insana boiled or roasted under ashes with oil, vinegar, and pepper, as people use to eat mushrooms. But I would rather wish English men to content themselves with the meat and sauce of our own country, than with fruit and sauce eaten with such peril: for doubtless these apples have a mischievous quality, the use of which is utterly to be forsaken. E The juice drawn forth from the roots, dried, and taken in small quantity, purges the belly exceedingly of phlegm and melancholic humors.
F It is good to be put into medicines and eye-washes (collyria) that ease the pain of the eyes; and used underneath as a pessary it draws forth the dead child and afterbirth.
G The green leaves, pounded with hog's grease and barley meal, cool all hot swellings and inflammations, and have the power to dissolve abscesses and hot ulcers when bruised and applied thereon.
H A suppository made with the same juice and inserted into the fundament causes sleep.
I The wine in which the root has been boiled or steeped provokes sleep and eases pain.
K The smell of the apples likewise induces sleep, but the juice works more effectively if taken in small quantity.
L Great and strange effects are supposed to be in mandrakes—to make women fruitful and bear children, if they but carry the same near their bodies. Some ground this belief on the fact that Rachel desired to have her sister's mandrakes (as the text is translated), but if we look well into the circumstances we shall find, we may rather judge otherwise. Young Reuben brought home lovely and sweet-smelling flowers (for so the Hebrew word signifies, which is used in Canticles 7:13 in the same sense), and the lad brought them home rather for their beauty and smell than for their virtue. Now in the flowers of the mandrake there is no such delightful or lovely smell as was in those pleasant flowers which Reuben brought home. Besides, we do not read that Rachel conceived as a result of this, for Leah, Jacob's wife, had four children before God granted that blessing of fruitfulness to Rachel. And last of all (which is my chief reason), Jacob was angry with Rachel when she said, "Give me children, or else I die," and asked her whether he were in the place of God, who had withheld from her the fruit of her body. And we know that the prophet David says, "Children and the fruit of the womb are an inheritance that comes from the Lord," Psalm 127.
